analysis.one_liner: Sets federal limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in baby food.
analysis.headline: The Baby Food Safety Act was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in December 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the FDA to set mandatory limits on four toxic heavy metals — lead, inorganic arsenic, cadmium, and mercury — in food made for babies and toddlers, including infant formula. Food exceeding those limits would be legally adulterated, and the FDA would gain authority to force a recall of contaminated baby food. The bill died in committee without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and babies. Heavy metals like lead and arsenic can harm infant brain development even at low levels, and today there are no binding federal limits for them in baby food. The bill would make food exceeding a set limit illegal to sell and give the FDA power to order recalls of contaminated products rather than relying on voluntary action by manufacturers.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA, by administrative order, to establish limits for lead, cadmium, mercury, and inorganic arsenic in infant and toddler food, defined to include infant formula.
Makes baby food in final product form that exceeds an established limit legally adulterated under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, so it cannot lawfully be sold.

Expands the FDA's existing mandatory recall authority to cover infant and toddler food containing toxic elements that render it adulterated, allowing the agency to force recalls rather than request them.

Sets statutory deadlines: proposed limits for lead, inorganic arsenic, and cadmium by the end of 2025 with final orders by mid-2027, and a slower track for mercury, while directing the FDA to keep limits 'as low as reasonably achievable' for each food type.

analysis.who_pays: Baby food manufacturers and their ingredient suppliers, who would have to test products, meet the limits, and pull contaminated batches off shelves. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to families in the form of higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for testing, reformulation, and supplier screening would fall on manufacturers and would likely be passed to consumers through higher baby food prices.

Heavy metals enter food from soil and water, so not all contamination can be eliminated; the bill acknowledges this by requiring feasibility-based limits for each food category, but some products could still become more expensive or scarce.

The bill sets statutory deadlines for regulators rather than letting the FDA set its own pace, and the slow track for mercury limits (proposed by 2029, final by 2030) reflects how much harder the science is for some elements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and specific: low-level exposure to lead and arsenic during infancy is linked to developmental harm, and there are currently no binding federal limits for these metals in baby food, only FDA guidance. The costs — testing and reformulation for manufacturers, modestly higher prices for parents — are genuine but targeted at a product category where safety failures carry lifelong consequences. The bill tried to soften the burden by letting the FDA tailor limits to what is achievable for each food type. On balance, the case for the bill is stronger than the case against it, which is what makes its quiet death in committee worth noting.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Baby Food Safety Act of 2023 was introduced on December 13, 2023 by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, joined by Reps. Cárdenas and Sykes.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and two days later to that committee's Subcommittee on Health.
That was the last action of any kind: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill's ten cosponsors were all House Democrats; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Baby food manufacturers are better off because the bill died: they face no binding federal limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, or mercury in their products and no expanded FDA recall power for this category. Parents of infants continue to rely on voluntary FDA guidance instead.

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill establishing mandatory toxic-element limits and mandatory recall authority for baby food.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or committee vote in the thirteen months it had jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: All ten cosponsors were Democrats and the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans, so the bill never crossed the aisle and never got a vote.

industries.note: The bill would require manufacturers to test for and stay under mandatory limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury, and would let the FDA force recalls of contaminated products. Their interest in avoiding binding limits and recall exposure runs against parents' interest in safe food.

industries.industry: Baby food ingredient suppliers and farming
industries.note: Heavy metals in crops come largely from soil and water, so growers and ingredient suppliers would face pressure to screen sources or shift sourcing. Some of that cost is genuine; some of it is the point of the bill.
